To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

for many diffusion processes and network topologies, the expected number of individuals reached by a random seed set is larger than the expected number of people reached by a set that optimally targets the best individuals in the network.

(i) for a large class of random networks and for some frequently studied information diffusion models, (ii) random seeding can be better than optimally targeting seeds, (iii) the difference between the two strategies is economically significant.

(1) the optimal set of seeds for a diffusion process on a network is not the set of individuals with the largest number of neighbors; and (2) the optimal set is also not the set of nodes that are most central in the network, in the sense of having the shortest average distance from every other node.
